h1: The 8 Best Monitors Under $300 of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: the 8 best monitors under $300, including QHD gaming panels, USB-C single-cable models, and a 4K office pick, compared on specs.
summary: The ASUS TUF Gaming VG27AQ3A is the best monitor under $300: 27 inch QHD at 180Hz with 1ms response and broad adaptive sync, in the $100 to $200 tier. The Dell S2725DSM is the cheapest route to QHD, and the Dell S2725DC adds 65W USB-C. The Philips is the 4K office pick and the LG 27G640A tops out at 300Hz.
intro: Under $300 you can now buy a QHD monitor with a fast refresh rate, which retires the old tradeoff between sharp and fast. The better question is what the screen is for. Gaming rewards refresh rate, laptop users want USB-C power delivery that actually charges the machine, and spreadsheet work wants pixel density and a stand that fits a desk.

We reviewed eight monitors on paper, comparing resolution, refresh rate, panel type and connectivity from the spec sheets. Several sit in a $200 to $500 bracket that straddles the cap, so check the live price before you buy. The pattern across the group is that a 300Hz panel and a 65W USB-C port are rarely found in the same box.

products.name: ASUS TUF Gaming VG27AQ3A 27-Inch QHD 180Hz
products.verdict: QHD at 180Hz with the broadest adaptive sync support.
products.description:
The ASUS TUF Gaming VG27AQ3A is a 27 inch QHD Fast IPS panel at 180Hz with a 1ms response time. It supports ELMB Sync, G-Sync compatibility and FreeSync Premium, covers 130% sRGB, handles HDR10 and includes built-in speakers. It sits in the $100 to $200 tier. Broad adaptive sync matters because it removes tearing on either brand of graphics card, so you are not locked to one GPU maker.

It leads because it delivers the best gaming performance per dollar while still serving as an everyday work screen. The LG 27G640A pushes 300Hz, but it costs more and needs a very strong GPU. The Dell S2725DSM costs less, but gives up 36Hz and the G-Sync label.

Buy it if you play games and work on the same screen. The caveat is that no USB-C input is listed, so a laptop needs a separate charger. Skip it if you want a single-cable dock.
products.idealFor: Gamers who also use the monitor for work.
products.skipIf: You want a single-cable laptop dock.

products.name: Dell 27 Plus QHD Monitor S2725DSM
products.verdict: QHD at 144Hz at the lowest price in the group.
products.description:
The Dell S2725DSM is a 27 inch QHD IPS monitor at 144Hz with a 1ms MPRT response, 1500:1 contrast and a 4-star TUV eye comfort rating. Dual 3W speakers and AMD FreeSync round it out, in the $100 to $200 tier. QHD at 27 inches gives text a noticeably finer edge than 1080p, and 144Hz is smooth enough for casual play.

It ranks second because it costs less than the ASUS and gives up 36Hz of refresh and the broader sync coverage. For office use and casual gaming that gap is small, and the Dell's eye comfort rating suits long workdays. Against the Dell S2725DC, it saves money but leaves out USB-C.

Choose it for the cheapest route to QHD. The caveat is the lower refresh rate and FreeSync-only sync: an Nvidia card owner who wants G-Sync should look at the ASUS. Skip it if you want a laptop dock.
products.idealFor: Budget buyers who want QHD sharpness.
products.skipIf: You use an Nvidia card and want G-Sync.

products.name: Dell 27 Plus QHD USB-C Monitor S2725DC
products.verdict: A real single-cable setup with 65W power delivery.
products.description:
The Dell S2725DC is a 27 inch QHD IPS monitor at 144Hz with 1ms MPRT. What it adds is USB-C with 65W power delivery, so one cable carries the picture and charges the laptop, plus a pop-out port panel for quick plug-ins. It sits in the $200 to $500 bracket. The 65W figure is enough to charge most thin laptops while sending video.

That wattage is why it beats the S2725DSM for laptop users: a one-cable desk replaces a charger, a video lead and a clutter of ports. Against the LG 27G640A, the Dell's 65W delivery is more than four times the LG's 15W, which only trickles.

Buy it if you work from a USB-C laptop. The caveat is that it costs more than the plain Dell, and the listing does not mention speakers. Skip it if you use a desktop only.
products.idealFor: Laptop users who want one cable.

products.name: Philips 27" 4K UHD USB-C Monitor 27E1N5900R
products.verdict: 4K sharpness and USB-C docking over gaming speed.
products.description:
The Philips 27E1N5900R is a 27 inch 4K UHD IPS panel at 3840 by 2160 with USB-C 65W power delivery, a USB 3.2 hub, DisplayHDR 400 and a 4-year advance replacement warranty. It sits in the $200 to $500 bracket. At 27 inches, 4K is dense enough that text and photo detail look crisp without scaling tricks.

It ranks below the Dell S2725DC because the refresh rate is not listed, which points to an office-first design, and it does not chase gaming speed. In return you get 4K clarity, a hub for peripherals and the longest warranty in this guide. The Dell wins on smoothness; the Philips wins on sharpness.

Choose it for documents, photo work and docking a laptop. The caveat is that it is not aimed at gamers. Skip it if you want a fast gaming panel.
products.idealFor: Office work and photo editing with a laptop.
products.skipIf: You want a fast gaming panel.

products.name: LG 27G640A-B UltraGear 27-Inch QHD 300Hz
products.verdict: The fastest refresh rate here, at 300Hz.
products.description:
The LG 27G640A-B UltraGear is a 27 inch QHD IPS monitor at 300Hz with 1ms response. It supports VESA DisplayHDR 400, covers 95% DCI-P3, and offers USB-C with 15W power delivery, dual HDMI 2.1 ports and DisplayPort 1.4. It sits in the $200 to $500 bracket. 300Hz refreshes the screen 300 times a second, which only helps if your graphics card can render that many frames.

It places lower in our ranking because the 300Hz headroom only pays off with a very strong graphics card, and the 15W USB-C cannot charge a laptop. The ASUS gives most of the gaming feel at 180Hz for far less.

Buy it if frame rate is your priority and you play competitive shooters. The caveat is that you need a powerful PC to use the speed. Skip it if you do not have a high-end graphics card.
products.skipIf: You do not have a high-end graphics card.

products.name: Samsung 32" Odyssey G5 (G50F) QHD Gaming Monitor
products.verdict: The largest QHD screen here, at 32 inches.
products.description:
The Samsung Odyssey G5 G50F is a 32 inch QHD Fast IPS display at 180Hz with 1ms GtG, HDR10, G-Sync compatibility and AMD FreeSync. It adds Black Equalizer and Virtual Aim Point gaming aids and sits in the $200 to $500 bracket. The 32 inch panel is the largest flat screen here, and it gives gamers a bigger field of view.

Compared with the 27 inch ASUS, it offers more screen at the same QHD resolution, which spreads the pixels over a larger area and makes them slightly less sharp. You sit farther back to compensate. Against the curved LG 32G600A, the Samsung's flat panel keeps straight lines straight and covers both sync standards.

Choose it for a bigger display and immersive play. The caveat is lower pixel density and the deeper desk space it needs. Skip it if your desk is shallow.
products.idealFor: Gamers who want a big screen.

products.name: LG 32G600A-B UltraGear 32-Inch Curved QHD
products.description:
The LG 32G600A-B is a 32 inch curved QHD IPS display with a 1000R curve, 180Hz, 1ms response, HDR10 and up to 99% sRGB. It supports AMD FreeSync and has a three-side virtually borderless design. It sits in the $200 to $500 bracket. A 1000R curve wraps the edge of the screen toward your eyes, which deepens the feeling of immersion in racing games and wide scenes.

It ranks seventh because the curve warps straight lines, which hurts spreadsheets, layouts and CAD, and the listing offers FreeSync only. Samsung's flat 32 inch gives broader sync support and a cleaner grid. Against the ASUS VG27AQ3A, you gain size and curve but lose adaptive sync breadth.

Buy it for immersive games and movies. The caveat is distortion for precise layout work. Skip it if you design, draw or build spreadsheets all day.
products.skipIf: You do design or CAD work.

products.name: ASUS VA27AQ 27-Inch QHD IPS
products.verdict: QHD sharpness for work at only 75Hz.
products.description:
The ASUS VA27AQ is a 27 inch QHD IPS monitor at 75Hz with 1ms response and 99% sRGB coverage. It has a frameless VESA-ready design and takes HDMI, DisplayPort and VGA inputs, plus built-in speakers. It sits in the $100 to $200 tier. The VGA port is a rarity on a new QHD screen and helps if you connect older equipment.

It lands last because 75Hz is slow next to the 144Hz Dell S2725DSM at a similar tier, and the ASUS TUF sits in the same tier with 180Hz and adaptive sync. What keeps it on the list is color accuracy for work and that legacy port.

Choose it for spreadsheets, documents and office use on a budget. The caveat is the refresh rate, so skip it if you play fast games. Check the live price, since the Dell S2725DSM may match it.

whatMatters.detail: QHD is 2560 by 1440 and 4K is 3840 by 2160. Higher resolution gives sharper text and finer photos on the same screen size, but needs a stronger GPU for games. Check the pixel count in the title or specs, and weigh it against size: 4K at 27 inches is far denser than QHD at 32. Text scaling in your operating system also matters.

Refresh is how many times the screen updates per second. 144Hz and above feels noticeably smoother for games, while 75Hz is fine for office work. Check the Hz figure in the bullets, and remember your graphics card must produce the frames: the LG 300Hz is wasted on a modest GPU. Most office work never needs more than 75Hz.

USB-C power delivery lets one cable carry video and charge a laptop. 65W suits thin laptops, while 15W only trickles power into a phone-class device. Check the wattage in the listing: the Dell S2725DC and Philips list 65W, the LG 27G640A only 15W. A laptop with a big charger may need more than 65W, so check its rating first.

G-Sync and FreeSync reduce tearing and stutter when the frame rate varies. Nvidia cards work best with G-Sync compatible displays, and AMD cards with FreeSync. Check which are listed: the ASUS TUF and Samsung list both, while the Dell S2725DSM and LG 32G600A list FreeSync only. A mismatched card still works, with fewer guarantees.

A 32 inch screen needs more desk depth, and a curve suits immersion but can distort straight lines. Match the size to your viewing distance: a 27 inch QHD panel suits a normal desk, while 32 inch works if you sit farther back. Check the dimensions and whether the stand fits your desk, and consider a monitor arm if depth is short.

faq.q: Will my laptop charge over USB-C?
faq.a: Only if the monitor delivers enough watts. The Dell S2725DC and Philips offer 65W, which suits thin laptops, while the LG 27G640A offers only 15W. Check your laptop charger's rating before relying on the monitor, because a heavy-duty workstation may need more.

Paying for 300Hz without a graphics card to match. The LG 27G640A only shines with a very strong GPU, while the ASUS VG27AQ3A delivers most of the smoothness at 180Hz for less, and a modest card cannot feed 300 frames anyway.

At 27 inches, yes. Text and images are noticeably sharper, which is why the Dell S2725DSM and ASUS VA27AQ both use QHD. For a bigger 32 inch screen like the Samsung's, QHD looks softer than on a 27 inch.

faq.q: How do I set refresh rate?
faq.a: Set it in your operating system display settings and use DisplayPort or HDMI 2.1 for high rates. The LG 27G640A lists both DisplayPort 1.4 and HDMI 2.1, while the ASUS VA27AQ at 75Hz needs no special cable. Plug into the graphics card, not the motherboard.
The ASUS VA27AQ lists a frameless VESA design. Check the listing for the others before you buy an arm, because not every curved or large monitor like the LG 32G600A supports a standard mount.

HDR400 modes help little compared with true HDR displays, so do not pay extra for it alone. The ASUS TUF, Philips and LG 27G640A list HDR10 or DisplayHDR 400, but color, contrast and refresh matter more for daily use.

finalTake: Buy the ASUS VG27AQ3A if you game and work on the same screen. Choose the Dell S2725DSM for the cheapest QHD, the Dell S2725DC for a one-cable laptop desk, and the Philips for 4K documents and photos. The LG 300Hz is for competitive players with a strong graphics card. Decide your main use first, because no monitor here wins every column.
